editorial.brief: Counter-Strike 2 is the one story that turns up in two places with money attached: 1,206,781 peak players on Steam, and two PGL Major Singapore matches drawing $1M apiece on Polymarket. Wikipedia went its own way, to Joe Milton at 385,182 views. Hacker News and Lemmy shared a single grim item, the states suing SpaceX over Grok.
editorial.cover_sub: Joe Milton drew 385,182 Wikipedia readers, 1.5 times the runner-up, on a Saturday when the other feeds were busy with Counter-Strike, Christmas playlists and a lawsuit against SpaceX.
editorial.wiki_deck: Joe Milton led Wikipedia by 135,363 views over a top-level domain. Nothing else in the snapshot says why, though a second footballer further down the list offers a hint.
editorial.letter_headline: A Saturday spent watching other people play
editorial.discourse_deck: Hacker News is admiring clever engineering and fretting over WebRTC card skimmers. Lemmy is angry about Grok, French teargas and the free market. Bluesky has striking Madrid teachers and Detroit pie. Mastodon has goats, clouds and dead malls.
editorial.foreign_deck: The wires had Asian stocks sliding on a faltering AI rebound and the UN calling for AI safety talks, while the world searched for lottery numbers, cricket and pizza.
editorial.markets_deck: Polymarket's largest book, $3M, gives a 25-basis-point December Fed cut no chance. Then come two Counter-Strike matches, a Taipei mayoralty at 57% and Hakeem Jeffries at zero.
editorial.watch_deck: Counter-Strike 2 peaked at 1,206,781 on Steam, ahead of Dota 2 at 804,636 and PUBG at 748,430. On Twitch, 加藤純一うん〇ちゃん held 136,893 viewers, more than three times TheBurntPeanut's 42,437.
editorial.yt_headline: Anuel AA's Los Diablos, as a visualizer
editorial.yt_note: Beneath 3.8 million views for Los Diablos sit a million-view dare called if you don't TIP you DIE and two Avengers: Doomsday theories about Doctor Doom. A Christmas playlist has arrived on schedule, with 342,762.
editorial.closing_note: By tomorrow, Stage 2 in Singapore will have new results, the Mega Millions numbers will be old, and the abandoned mall will wait another year for its post. Joe Milton may keep his readers or lose them to the next name. The Fed market will still be at zero, which counts as continuity.
wiki_paras: Joe Milton was Wikipedia's most-read article, with 385,182 views. Second place went to .xxx, the internet domain set aside for adult sites, at 249,819. That is a lead of 1.5 times, comfortable rather than crushing. Ramayana: Part 1 took third with 229,774, and the perennial Deaths in 2026 sat fourth at 127,653.

The snapshot does not say what Milton did. No wire headline mentions him, and his name appears in none of the social feeds. The only clue is in fifth place: Mason Rudolph, filed under American football, with 117,924 views. Two footballers in one top five suggests a single game or roster decision that nobody here thought to post about.

Set against the rest of the day, the result looks private. Steam and Polymarket were occupied with Counter-Strike, and YouTube with Avengers: Doomsday and Christmas songs. Wikipedia readers were looking up a quarterback. The encyclopedia is still where people go when they hear a name in passing and want to know whose it is.
letter_paras: This was a scattered day with one thread running through it. Counter-Strike 2 peaked at 1,206,781 players on Steam while bettors put $1M each on Astralis against Imperial and G2 against Liquid. Beyond that, the feeds kept to themselves: a quarterback on Wikipedia, pizza on Google in Brazil and Britain, and a reggaeton visualizer on YouTube.

The smaller corners repaid attention. USGS logged 25 quakes above magnitude 2.5, the largest a 5.2 some 93 km west of San Antonio de los Cobres in Argentina. Japan searched for tornado advisories. On Mastodon, one poster marked the 57th birthday of the Muppets' Mahna Mahna, and another put up an abandoned mall, described as an annual Black Friday obligation.

Taking the reading at the same hour each day removes timing as an excuse. If pizza leads in two countries on a Saturday, that is a fact about Saturdays, not about when the editor woke up. Over months the snapshots stop being anecdotes and become a record, one that shows which subjects come back and which, like most of today's, do not.
